[PURPOSE]: To demonstrate the feasibility of in vivo monitoring of the myogenic differentiation process from human muscle precursor cells to mature skeletal muscle tissue by measuring characteristic magnetic resonance (MR) imaging relaxation and diffusion properties as a potential noninvasive diagnostic tool in muscle cell therapy.
[MATERIALS AND METHODS]: The study was approved by the ethics committee for studies in humans and the animal care committee. The hypothesis was tested by means of subcutaneous injection of human muscle precursor cells from the rectus abdominis muscle into nude mice (n = 18). Animals injected with human fibroblasts, prostate cancer cells, or collagen served as control animals (four in each group). The muscle precursor cells exhibited a nonspecific pattern compared with that in control animals in the early stages. During differentiation, the relaxation and diffusion parameters decreased and approached the values for mature skeletal muscle tissue: T1, 1386 msec ± 88; T2, 32.0 msec ± 4.3; T2*, 10.8 msec ± 0.8; ADC, 1.39 × 10(-3) mm(2)/sec ± 0.02 (reference erector spinae muscle tissue: T1, 1417 msec ± 106; T2, 31.0 msec ± 2.4; T2*, 11.3 msec ± 1.7; and ADC, 1.40 × 10(-3) mm(2)/sec ± 0.03).
[CONCLUSION]: MR imaging relaxation and diffusion measurements can be used as potential biomarkers for noninvasive in vivo monitoring of the myogenic differentiation process from muscle precursor cells to mature skeletal muscle tissue in muscle cell therapy.

key_findings.finding: A primary in-vivo study (PMID 25423144, Radiology 2015) directly supports quantitative MRI characterization of myogenic differentiation: human rectus-abdominis muscle precursor cells were injected subcutaneously into nude mice, and serial 4.7-T T1, T2, T2*, and ADC measurements changed from high early-stage values toward mature skeletal-muscle values (T1 2242→1386 ms; T2 224→32 ms; T2* 33.3→10.8 ms; ADC 1.53→1.39×10−3 mm²/s). The engineered tissue was biologically validated with immunofluorescence, Western blot, and contraction assays, with fibroblast, prostate-cancer-cell, and collagen controls. This is direct evidence for noninvasive characterization of differentiation, although the abstract does not provide the specific marker identities or full time-course/statistical details.

source_tools.relevance: Primary study abstract with design, quantitative T1/T2/T2*/ADC findings, controls, and biological validation

key_findings.finding: The available evidence is concentrated in this single direct relaxometry study; a contemporaneous commentary explicitly interprets MR relaxation and diffusion measurements as detecting implanted human muscle precursor-cell differentiation into mature skeletal muscle (PMID 25710336). Searches did not identify comparable in-vivo T1/T2/T2* studies specifically validating satellite-cell differentiation.

source_tools.relevance: Commentary summarizing the direct differentiation study
Satellite-cell-focused search results, which returned no direct relaxometry differentiation primary study among the relevant records

key_findings.finding: MRI can also track transplanted myoblast grafts without proving differentiation: ferritin-engineered C2C12 skeletal myoblasts produced T2 shortening in vitro and hypointense grafts in infarcted mouse hearts; MRI-estimated graft size correlated with histology (R²=0.8), while separate assays showed ferritin did not impair viability, proliferation, or differentiation. This supports localization/graft-size monitoring, not a direct MRI-based readout of differentiation state.

source_tools.relevance: Primary ferritin-MRI myoblast tracking study abstract with T2 effect, in-vivo detection, histologic correlation, and differentiation assay

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: quantitative relaxometry (especially combined T1/T2/T2* with diffusion) is feasible for noninvasive, label-free characterization of in-vivo differentiation of transplanted human muscle precursor cells when paired with tissue-level validation; however, relaxation changes are not intrinsically specific for differentiation and should not be interpreted as proof without histology/immunostaining and/or functional validation. Most other MRI cell-therapy studies identified concern localization, viability, migration, graft size, or injury/repair rather than direct differentiation.

source_tools.relevance: Search results distinguishing the direct relaxometry paper from unrelated tracking/repair studies
